Ontario in concrete

Two brutalist routes, eleven stops. Part 1 covers the campuses built during the 1960s university boom, from the Niagara Peninsula through Waterloo, Guelph and Toronto to Trent. Part 2 carries on east through Kingston, Ottawa and Gatineau and ends in Montreal.

  3. 3GuelphGuelphabout 1 h 15 to York
  4. 4YorkTorontoabout 1 h 45 to Trent

Day 2

1

Brock University

St. Catharines

Start with the tower. Schmon Tower sits at the centre of a terraced concrete complex, and the rest of the core campus is organised around it.

  • Schmon Tower: 1968
  • Mackenzie Chown Complex: 1972, by Raymond Moriyama

Arthur Schmon Tower and the Thistle Complex

1968

The tower has 13 floors. Six of them hold the James A. Gibson Library, and senior administration is on the top floor. The Thistle Complex is the low, stepped mass around its base, with lecture halls and the Sean O'Sullivan Theatre as its focal point.

Go down to the underground level, where Market Hall runs beneath the building. It is the best place on campus to see the concrete from inside.

Mackenzie Chown Complex

1972, Raymond Moriyama

Moriyama was also a Brock chancellor. The long, banded academic block is a good contrast with the vertical tower: the same concrete, laid out horizontally across the landscape.

Brock to Waterlooabout 1 h 45 by car, off-peak
2

University of Waterloo

Waterloo

Waterloo's concrete is scattered across a campus of many styles, so this stop is two main buildings and a short walk between them.

  • Dana Porter Library: opened 1965, extended to ten storeys by about 1970
  • Architects: Shore & Moffat and Partners

Dana Porter Library

1965, extended by 1970 · Shore & Moffat and Partners

It opened as the Arts Library and was named for Dana Porter, the university's first chancellor, in 1967. The upper floors were added soon after the first stage, which turned a seven-storey block into a ten-storey one. Students call it the sugar cube. Look at the funnel-shaped pillars at the base, which frame the façade.

Mathematics and Computer building (MC)

Built during the 1960s expansion

MC is widely named as one of Waterloo's strongest brutalist buildings. The ribbed concrete skin is the thing to photograph, especially in raking light.

Also nearby. Modern Languages opened in 1965 as the Arts building and is part of the same early expansion. I couldn't confirm how brutalist it reads, so treat it as a short detour rather than a stop.
Waterloo to Guelphabout 35 min by car, off-peak
3

University of Guelph

Guelph

Guelph put up five concrete buildings in three years in the 1960s. They sit beside an older stone campus, which makes the contrast easy to read.

  • South Residence: John Andrews, commissioned 1966
  • McLaughlin Library: 1968
  • Expansion overseen by: Josep Lluís Sert

South Residence (originally Complex B)

John Andrews, commissioned 1966

Andrews had just finished Scarborough College, and here he built a long, low residence that reads as a concrete landscape rather than a tower. Local legend says a prison architect designed it. The architect was Andrews, and the building set a new model for residence life in Canada.

No photo hereI couldn't find a freely licensed photo of South Residence. The University of Guelph Library's brutalism exhibit has period photos and the full story.

MacNaughton Building

1960s expansion

One of the Sert-era concrete buildings, with angled walls and richly textured concrete. One student writer called it a favourite. Stand where you can see it against the older stone buildings on the green.

McLaughlin Library

1968

The interior has been renovated, so the concrete shell is the draw here. Visitor access follows the library's hours.

Check before you go. MacKinnon is the other Sert-era building to see. It has been through renovation planning, so confirm what is accessible.
Guelph to Yorkabout 1 h 15 by car, off-peak
4

York University

Keele campus, Toronto

York's original core is the densest cluster on the route. Many of the buildings came from one planning firm, so they read as a single composition.

  • Ross Building: opened 1968, nine storeys
  • Designed by: UPACE, the firm formed in 1962 for York's master plan
  • Transit: York University subway station, since 2017

Ross Social Sciences and Humanities Building

1968 · UPACE

The Ross Building is the centrepiece: a nine-storey grid of concrete in two sections, joined by an archway between Ross North and Ross South. Inside it is a maze of courtyards, with a sunken student lounge. An open terrace links it to Scott Library.

The big concrete ramp that once led to the east entrance was removed in 1988. Vari Hall (1992, postmodernist) now stands there and hides part of the building, so walk around to see Ross as it was meant to be seen.

Scott Library

UPACE

The largest building on campus, shaped like an inverted ziggurat, with each floor stepping out over the one below. The interior has a zigzag staircase and is worth walking through while the library is open.

Curtis Lecture Halls

Part of York's original concrete core

The lecture halls are tiered rooms inside the concrete shell. If one is open between classes, step in.

If you have time. York's student-built architecture guide also lists Osgoode Hall Law School and the Petrie Science and Engineering Building in the same set.
York to Trentabout 1 h 45 by car, off-peak
5

Trent University

Peterborough

End on the river. Ron Thom planned the whole campus, and it is laid out along the Otonabee River.

  • Bata Library: opened 1969
  • Architect: Ron Thom, master planner
  • Faryon Bridge: Paul Merrick

Bata Library

1969 · Ron Thom

The library is the centrepiece, with a four-storey façade made of vertical bastions and each level looking down to the river. The rubble aggregate walls invite touching.

Champlain College and Lady Eaton College

Ron Thom

Champlain is the campus centrepiece across the main square from the library, with a remarkable ceiling in its Great Hall. Lady Eaton College is east of the main court and known for its wooden chandeliers. Thom specified almost everything inside, down to the lamp bases. The Chemistry Building completes the original set.

Faryon Bridge

Paul Merrick, Thom's business partner

The concrete bridge joins the east and west banks of the campus. It shared a national design award with Champlain College in 1971.

Walk it with a guide. Trent's heritage site publishes a Ron Thom walking tour. Otonabee College, east of the science complex, was added later by a different architect.

Part 2: The capital and beyond

The second route picks up where Trent ends and follows the 401 corridor east. It starts with Queen's in Kingston, spends two days in Ottawa, crosses the river into Gatineau, and finishes in Montreal.

Trent to Kingstonabout 1 h 45 by car, off-peak
6

Queen's University

Kingston

Queen's is known for its limestone, which is why its concrete buildings stand out. Three halls from the early 1970s form the brutalist set.

  • Mackintosh-Corry Hall: 1973
  • Also: Jeffery Hall and John Watson Hall

Mackintosh-Corry Hall

1973

Mac-Corry went up on the former site of the George Richardson Memorial Stadium. The student paper calls its design a forgotten future, and says its confusing layout is a common complaint.

No photo hereI couldn't find freely licensed photos of Queen's brutalist buildings. The Queen's Journal piece on Mac-Corry's design has context and its own photos.

Jeffery Hall

Nicknamed "the bunker"

Some professors and students call Jeffery Hall the bunker. It is one of the three halls the student paper groups together as the campus's brutalist set.

John Watson Hall

Concrete exterior

Watson Hall's concrete exterior is a surprise against the limestone around it. The entrance from University Avenue is awkward, which suits the style's habit of ignoring its surroundings.

Not on this list. Stauffer Library looks like it might belong, but it opened in 1994 as a postmodern design with neo-Gothic influences. Skip it for this tour.
Kingston to Ottawaabout 2 h by car, off-peak
7

Carleton University

Ottawa

Carleton's 1960s and 70s buildings are linked by tunnels, which makes it the best stop on the route for a cold day.

  • Architecture Building: late 1960s
  • Loeb Building: by James Strutt

Architecture Building

Late 1960s

Carleton's school of architecture is a late-1960s brutalist building laid out on a strict tartan grid, with a central sunken space and two interior streets crossing it. Sources disagree on whether it was finished in 1968 or 1972.

Loeb Building

James Strutt

Loeb is three linked, offset towers, and it connects to the campus tunnel network. It is brick-faced rather than bare concrete, so it reads softer than the others.

Dunton Tower

Carleton's tallest tower

Dunton Tower stands at the edge of the Rideau Canal. I haven't confirmed how brutalist it reads, so treat it as a stop for the view rather than a headline.

Check before you go. The campus master plan recommended demolishing Paterson Hall in 2016. I couldn't confirm what happened, so see whether it is still there. I also haven't verified Southam Hall.
Carleton to Tunney's Pasturea short drive within Ottawa
8

Tunney's Pasture

Ottawa

A federal office campus built in the 1960s and 70s. Two towers dominate it and you can see both from far off.

  • R.H. Coats: 1976, 26 storeys
  • Brooke Claxton: 19 storeys, designed by two national partnerships

R.H. Coats Building

1976 · Ogilvie and Hogg

A 26-storey, 99 m office tower and the tallest in the complex. It houses Statistics Canada. It stands beside the Tunney's Pasture transit station, so you can see it the moment you step off.

Brooke Claxton Building

19 storeys

A 19-storey tower in the Modern International style with aspects of Brutalism. It was planned as the focal point of the campus, at the corner of Columbine Boulevard and Holland Avenue. Its height broke through the 150-foot limit that then applied downtown.

Etiquette. This is a working federal campus. Stay on public sidewalks and shoot from outside.
Tunney's Pasture to downtown Ottawaabout 15 min by car, off-peak
9

Downtown Ottawa and uOttawa

Ottawa

A cluster of civic and federal concrete in the core, mostly within short walks of each other, with uOttawa's library a short hop east.

  • National Arts Centre: 1967
  • Pearson Building: 1973
  • Library main branch: open through 2027

Pearkes Building

National Defence Headquarters · 101 Colonel By Dr

Pearkes is the main base of National Defence Headquarters, and one of the major brutalist office blocks in the core. It faces Confederation Park, so you can see it across the green. It was planned as the first phase of the redevelopment that produced the Rideau Centre.

Ottawa Public Library main branch

120 Metcalfe St

The library has stayed open on a lease that runs to the end of 2027, because its replacement, Ādisōke, has been delayed. Go before it moves.

National Arts Centre

1967 · Fred Lebensold

Built for the centennial in geometric precast concrete with very few windows. Diamond Schmitt's renovation added a lot of glass and a hexagonal marquee tower, the Kipnes Lantern, and kept some original features such as the terrazzo floors. Expect a softened version of the original.

Lester B. Pearson Building

1973 · 125 Sussex Dr

Global Affairs Canada's headquarters, designed by Webb Zerafa Menkès Housden. Stepped, dark concrete masses that are most impressive from across the street.

University of Ottawa: Morisset Library

A short trip east

Morisset appears on a list of notable brutalist libraries in Canada. The entrance is the best part to see. Vanier Hall (1973) is also named as an example of academic brutalism, though I only found that on a weak source.

Downtown Ottawa to Gatineauminutes by car across the river
10

Gatineau

Quebec

Cross the Ottawa River into Quebec. The Portage complex looks back across the water at Parliament Hill.

  • Place du Portage III: 1973 to 1978
  • Maison du Citoyen: inaugurated 1980

Place du Portage III

1973 to 1978 · David, Boulva and Dimakopoulos

A megastructure of six connected towers in two stepped blocks on either side of Boulevard Maisonneuve, joined by a covered three-storey pedestrian bridge. It is one of the largest federal office buildings in Canada and a recognized federal heritage building.

See it soon. A renewal project is replacing the brutalist exterior with a lighter skin, so check its current state before you go.

Place du Portage IV

140 Promenade du Portage

A reinforced concrete megastructure that blends Brutalist and High-Tech influences. Look for the stepped masses and the roof terraces with built-in planters.

Maison du Citoyen

Hull's city hall · Daniel Lazosky and Pierre Cayer

The city hall of Gatineau stands at 25 Laurier Street. Construction started in 1978 and it was inaugurated in 1980. One travel guide calls its architecture aggressively brutalist.

No photo hereI couldn't find a clear, freely licensed exterior photo of the Maison du Citoyen.
Gatineau to Montrealabout 2 h by car, off-peak
11

Montreal

Quebec

End in Montreal, which has a reputation as one of the leading brutalist cities in North America.

  • Place Bonaventure: 1967
  • Habitat 67: 1967, Moshe Safdie
  • UQAM Judith-Jasmin: 1979

Place Bonaventure

1967 · Affleck, Desbarats, Dimakopoulos, Lebensold and Sise

A huge multi-purpose complex of offices, shops, exhibition space and a hotel at 800 de la Gauchetière Ouest. One critic called it a somewhat forbidding example of Brutalism. It was renovated in 1998, and it connects to the underground city.

UQAM: Pavillon Judith-Jasmin

1979 · Dimitri Dimakopoulos

The brick exterior makes this a brutalist building in materials other than plain concrete, though the interior is still largely concrete. It sits beside the spire of the Saint-Jacques church, which makes a strong contrast.

Habitat 67

1967 · Moshe Safdie

Built for Expo 67 as experimental modular housing, with 354 stacked concrete cubes. It is often called brutalist but breaks the style's usual rigid blocks. It is a residential complex, so view it from the street or across the water.

Keep going. Montreal has a lot more, including the Tour de la Bourse and several Metro stations. The Blue Crow Media Concrete Montreal Map, by France Vanlaethem with photography by Raphaël Thibodeau, selects about fifty buildings.

Before you go

  • Drive times are rough estimates for off-peak travel. Check live traffic, especially around Toronto.
  • Campus exteriors are open to walk. Interiors, libraries and lecture halls follow academic hours and may be locked on weekends.
  • Renovations change access. Check each campus's own news page for closures.
  • Gatineau and Montreal are in Quebec, where signage and service are in French first.
  • Tunney's Pasture, Pearkes, Pearson and the Place du Portage towers are working federal offices. Stay on public sidewalks and photograph from outside.
